rv.q: Icke brilliantly remakes Sophocles’ profoundly disturbing tragedy for our times.
An old play is masterfully analysed and made newly devastating.
At the risk of blurting out the worst-kept spoiler in theatre history, this show is mother**in’ good.
Yet overall the mighty momentum of the tragedy is thrilling in its grim inexorability.
The truth is literally blinding, here – and deafening, too
The piece has a cumulative power that builds gradually until the atmosphere is riveting, suffocating and unbearably tense.
It’s not the audacious invention of absolute peak Icke, but it is, nonetheless, really bloody good, with two astonishing leads.
For all the clock’s doomy marking down, this production fails to exert that grip for lengthy periods of time.
But the first requirement of a tragedy, surely, is that it should hold an audience transfixed: if we feel manipulated, tension seeps away.
If his stories tend to end unhappily, they also tend to send you reeling out into the night in the best sort of way.
The work by Manville and Strong at the end of the play is at once electrifying, and heartbreaking.
Such disconnection renders the final revelation trivial.

The result, helped by magnificent performances from Strong and Lesley Manville as his wife Jocasta, is as gripping as a thriller, yet weighted with the terrible sense (emphasised in a surprisingly tender epilogue) of what might have been.
